body.text: “Victoria November 2026: an election of dread”

When Victorians head to the polls on the last Saturday of next month, all the indications are that they will usher in that relatively rare thing — a change of state government. The twelve-year-old Labor administration, led by the recently installed Ben Carroll, is widely predicted to be unsentimentally flung from office.

That expectation might typically engender anticipation of a fresh beginning and reinvigoration. Yet the political atmosphere in Victoria is a long way from optimism. If the mood of the state’s citizens were to be summed up, it would be a mixture of fury, sullenness and despair overlaid with an element of impending dread.

All elections are, of course, distinctive. But as a longtime observer of Victorian politics, I have to say this one feels strikingly uncommon, at least in living memory, at two levels. First, as opinion polls consistently show, this is a genuine three-party contest, or perhaps more accurately three and a half: Labor versus the Coalition versus Pauline Hanson’s One Nation, with the Greens representing the extra half. And second, the public’s disenchantment with the choices on offer is unusually intense.

The disillusionent is especially directed towards the major parties, Labor and Liberal. According to the polls, neither can be confident of winning 30 per cent of the primary vote. The anger at incumbent Labor is particularly fierce: very few can objectively believe it deserves another term.

In fact, you need to go a long way back to find an election in which the party holding office was so discredited in the eyes of voters. The nearest approximation is Labor at the end of the Cain–Kirner era in the early 1990s when, with the state battered by economic recession and roiled by industrial strife, the ALP was brutally and effectively tarred as the “Guilty Party” in Liberal Party advertising.

And yet this ire hasn’t sent voters into the arms of the Liberal Party. Years of internecine squabbling, leadership chaos and policy negligence have created abiding distrust of the Liberals as a viable alternative government. By way of contrast, One Nation, a party that historically has attracted derisory levels of support in Victoria, is generating enthusiasm within sections of the electorate. But that seems driven more by a blow-everything-up nihilism than a genuine conviction that the party represents a constructive option for running the state.
In short, what we have in Victoria is a powerful pox-on-all-houses sentiment. Voters feel cheated.

How unprecedented is this? Interestingly, in some ways, it resonates with the patterns of Victorian state politics that prevailed during large parts of the first half of the twentieth century. The state’s politics during that period were peculiarly retrograde compared to most of the other states, mainly because of its triangular party system (Labor versus Liberal — or its earlier iterations — versus Country Party), which translated into chronic instability, cynical deal-making and unproductive governance. Victorian politics might be said to be in danger of regressing to that ugly past — to a time, long expunged from its citizens’ memory, that doesn’t fit with the state’s self-perception as the nation’s heartland of civilised progressivism.

Putting that awkward scenario aside, this election — which has significant chance of raising One Nation to a share in government — does feel “unVictorian” when measured against the state’s better-known political traditions. Beginning in the latter nineteenth century, Victoria became associated with a distinctive social-liberal style of politics, as expressed in its internationally eye-catching experiments in government intervention to improve the lot of citizens and harmonise life chances. It was colonial Victoria, for instance, that pioneered independent wage-fixing, workplace regulation and rudimentary welfare supports.

One of the torchbearers of that progressive liberalism was Alfred Deakin, later a three-time prime minister in the first decade of the Commonwealth, who more than anyone else was responsible for transplanting these innovations onto the new nation. A great Victorian, Deakin was so much more than the white supremacist he has been reduced to in some crude contemporary representations.

Though it was dormant for long stretches of the twentieth century, that social liberal tradition was revived during the remarkably modernising Liberal premiership of Rupert Hamer in the 1970s. Hamer’s government introduced a raft of progressive reforms in areas including education, the arts, the environment and consumer protection. It passed trailblazing equality of opportunity legislation, abolished capital punishment and decriminalised homosexual acts. When Hamer died in 2004 he was eulogised by Labor elder statesman Barry Jones as “the finest flower in the Victorian Deakinite liberal tradition.”

Following Hamer, though, the progressive social liberal–social democratic stream in Victorian politics was effectively co-opted by Labor, which had undergone its own dramatic remaking in the 1970s. The changing philosophical and political order in Victoria first materialised during John Cain’s premiership in the 1980s and subsequently in the twenty-first century under Steve Bracks and Daniel Andrews. The fact that Labor became chief custodian of the progressive, reformist traditions of Victorian politics from the late twentieth century surely goes a long way to explaining why it has enjoyed political hegemony in the state for much of the past fifty years. Labor hewed closer to Victoria’s defining political sensibility than did the Liberal Party.

The Victorian Liberals, meanwhile, were drifting towards the conservative right, emulating the changing philosophical disposition of the national party, which was spearheaded by the New South Wales branch and entrenched during John Howard’s prime ministership. The Victorian Liberals’ journey to the right, reinforced by influxes of Christian conservatives into its ranks and licensed by an aged, white, male base, increasingly estranged the party from the state’s voters. The evidence showed in state and federal election results, an underperformance that in turn cost the Victorians sway within the federal party.

Where once the Liberal Party was dominated by Victorians — beginning with its founder and prime-ministerial eminence, Robert Menzies — by the twenty-first century the state’s influence had vastly diminished. No Victorian has been federal leader since Andrew Peacock in 1990 — a staggering reversal of the state’s virtual monopoly over the Liberal leadership during its first forty-five years.

Eventually the growing philosophical mismatch between Victorians and the Liberal Party conditioned the party to write off the state as a kind of inhospitable “woke” outpost. Howard labelled Victoria “the Massachusetts of Australia” following Daniel Andrews’s crushing victory over the Coalition at the 2018 state election: a coded way of saying the state was unamenable to the brand of muscular conservatism he had done so much to imbue in the Liberal Party. As George Megalogenis astutely observes in his new book, Three Shocks, treating Victoria, and especially Melbourne, as somehow electorally expendable was a major miscalculation and an important reason for the cul de sac the party finds itself in.

The terrible irony of this story of modern Victorian politics — as bastion of progressive politics nationally but cold-shouldered by the Liberals as they pivoted rightwards — is that the state now appears poised to grant One Nation its greatest electoral breakthrough to date and perhaps, in a first for a populist party in Australia, a foothold in government. All this feels profoundly aberrant, as if the electorate is turning against its own nature.

How on earth has this come to pass in Victoria? The most obvious cause is general disgust at Labor’s performance in government. After a dozen years it is widely viewed to have grievously mismanaged the state’s finances, accumulating the highest public debt level in the nation. Still more damagingly, it faces alarming allegations of industrial-scale rorting and waste of public funds on its signature Big Build transport infrastructure projects.

The community’s seething at Labor might be explicable for those reasons alone, but other factors have also fuelled a venomous attitude to the government and the long shadow of Daniel Andrews. One is the undeniable, if difficult to quantify, effects of the Covid lockdowns, which eroded community civility and unleashed foetid and irrational conspiracy-style thinking within some (small) sections of the community. Malevolent theories have ricocheted around the community, amplified by the anti-social instruments of social media.

The virulent antagonism towards Labor and particularly Andrews has also been fed by parts of the mainstream media, most notably the Murdoch outlets. Their loathing of Andrews, which surfaced early in his premiership, seems to have originated principally in the fact that he was a formidable left-of-centre political force: a bold activist as premier, an excellent communicator and a phenomenon at the ballot box. Plus, he thumbed his nose at them.

These outlets barely disguised how much they despised Andrews and routinely indulged in their own conspiracy-making. Most conspicuous was the Herald Sun’s relentless stoking of the “Bike Boy” 2013 road accident episode, despite a police investigation having cleared Andrews and his wife of any wrongdoing. Offensive misinformation was hinted at in reporting of the premier’s 2021 fall, which left him with a serious back injury.

But the apotheosis of the Murdoch media’s aggressive campaign was probably Peta Credlin’s November 2022 Sky News exposé, “The Cult of Dan Andrews,” which feverishly characterised him as a local version of North Korea’s Kim Jong-un, a supreme leader untethered from democratic constraints. This “documentary” was screened shortly before he handsomely won a third election: how the Murdoch media’s collective teeth ground.

This is not to say Andrews was without grave faults as premier. Over time, supported by a powerful and overbearing private office, he badly overreached. His governing mantra of “getting shit done,” born of the lessons Labor took from the dying days of John Brumby’s government, in which Andrews was a minister, and the painfully inert 2010–14 administration of his immediate predecessors, Liberals Ted Baillieu and Denis Napthine, gradually morphed into something darker. Andrews trampled processes and suppressed dissenting voices in his own government. He chafed at accountability, and his instinct under pressure was to double down on his position and effectively declare “nothing to see here.”

Major follies under his watch included extravagant plans for the 2026 Commonwealth Games, which had to be abruptly cancelled in mid-2023 at great cost to taxpayers. Whether the squandering of public monies and the criminality on the Big Build projects has been of the gargantuan magnitude that has become embedded in the consciousness of Victorians through continual untested repetition and who is to blame might only really be fully revealed when the recently appointed royal commission has finished its work. It is unlikely, though, to paint a pretty picture.

Perhaps Andrews — like Kevin Rudd, whose instinctive preference for small-circle governing was reinforced during the global financial crisis —fell into the trap of not adjusting his ways after shouldering so much authority during the pandemic. In short, that emergency period exacerbated an existing predilection for unilateralism. That said, his ministers must share responsibility: they had a collective obligation to better restrain him regardless of how intimidating he and his office were.

For all that, the anti-Andrews pile-on, which has since spread to the Nine newspapers, has unquestionably tipped into hyperbolic territory. The stooped Andrews is now commonly rendered as an evil genius of Victorian politics who visited little more than disaster on the state. Yet his accomplishments were significant: he won three consecutive elections to become the longest-serving Labor premier and third-longest-serving premier in the state’s history; he was a highly popular leader who for much of his nine-year tenure was virtually politically untouchable; and he left a legacy that encompasses a massive upgrade of the state’s transport infrastructure and progressive reforms such as leading the nation in the introduction of voluntary assisted dying laws and negotiating a treaty with First Nations peoples.

The febrile, almost unhinged, attitude to Andrews was highlighted by a recent unedifying debate over the commissioning of a statue of him. Having met the benchmark created by his Liberal predecessor Jeff Kennett— 3000 days in office — he had qualified to be placed in the state premiers’ avenue of honour outside 1 Treasury Place. The free-for-all over the statue, which was eventually cancelled by a browbeaten Ben Carroll, was exemplified by federal Liberal shadow treasurer Tim Wilson’s declaration that a statue of Andrews was “at risk” of becoming “a public urinal.” Classy, indeed.

The extreme antagonism to Andrews was projected onto his successor, Jacinta Allan, after she inherited the premiership in September 2023. Unable to bring Andrews low, elements of the media and community refocused their pent-up antagonisms on Allan. Hers was an underwhelming premiership bedevilled by her incapacity to develop a distinctive leadership persona and serious misjudgements, not least her stubborn and almost unfathomable denial of the inevitability of initiating an inquiry into the Big Build scandals. Yet the visceral hostility to Allan, unquestionably tinged by gender prejudice, was disturbing.

Indeed, it’s notable that her departure in late July has allowed something of a cooling of the political temperature in Victoria, with her emollient replacement, Carroll, spending much of his brief time as premier apologising for the mistakes of his predecessors and distancing himself from them.

As the November election approaches, a final tantalising issue hangs over the national implications of the result. If it marks a major watershed for the populist right of Australian politics, with One Nation able to claim a place in a minority government with the Coalition, will Victoria be seen as a canary in the Australian political coal-mine and a harbinger of the next federal election? Or are circumstances so peculiarly rancid in Victoria — the mood so singularly distempered — that the state election won’t offer a reliable gauge of Australia’s immediate political future? In other words, should the Victorian election be treated as a sui generis affair?

Federal Labor is reportedly hoping that any carnage caused by an unholy governing alliance between One Nation and the Coalition would rapidly sober up the national polity. By this calculation, Victoria’s experience would inoculate Australia from the spread of the populist contagion. Of course, this is quite possibly wishful thinking. But we can safely say that if the inexperienced, thirty-six-year-old Liberal leader, Jess Wilson — opposition leader only since last November — becomes premier (and treasurer, as she intends) in a government dependent on One Nation she will be greatly tested.

Despite the Liberal leader’s sincere protestations of sensible moderation, we know that a Wilson government is pledged to repeal within a hundred days the Indigenous treaty legislation, painstakingly negotiated over nearly a decade, that her party has gratuitously cast as “divisive.” Rather than being sensible or moderate, that would be mindless and mean-spirited. It also belies her position as the solitary Victorian Liberal MP to have publicly supported the Indigenous Voice to Parliament.

That repeal might be a portent of the pressure Wilson will face to dance to the tune of powerful hardline conservative forces within the Liberal Party. Allied with this is the unavoidable question of how she will manage a Liberal party room riven for years by savage personal and ideological conflicts, on the one hand, while coping with One Nation, a byword for divisiveness, intolerance, spite and irrationality, on the other.

Let’s not join in the hyperbole by suggesting the barbarians are at the gate. But, just in case, cue an adapted version of the anguished cry of Macduff in Shakespeare’s Macbeth: “Oh Victoria, Victoria!” •
